newsitem.title: JORDAN: Jordan seeks $600 mln Paris Club debt rescheduling.
newsitem.headline: Jordan seeks $600 mln Paris Club debt rescheduling.

text.p: Jordan hopes to conclude a deal this week to reschedule the last $600 million tranche of over $3.5 billion of debt owed to Western creditors, Deputy Central Bank Governor Michel Marto said on Tuesday.

Marto said the talks with the Paris Club creditors due to start on Thursday were the fourth major and final rescheduling round, completing the restructuring of the $3.5-$4.0 billion debt incurred in the 1980s.
Economists say a favourable rescheduling is essential to push ahead with Jordan's economic reforms.
"We expect to conclude an exit rescheduling deal with the Paris Club for around $600 million of our debt on very favourable terms over a long period," Marto told Reuters.
Jordanian officials had earlier said the deal would cover $1.2 billion of debts.
The deal would reschedule outstanding principal and interest payments due between May 1997 to February 1999, Marto said.
Jordan's first restructuring of its debt was in 1989 after an economic crisis which forced the International Monetary Fund to intervene when the kingdom failed to service $8 billion of foreign debt.

After the disruption of the 1990 Gulf crisis, rescheduling was restarted with a February 1992 accord. The last major accord in June 1994 rescheduled $1.2 billion of the kingdom's debts over 20 years, including 10 years' grace period. A limited accord last October rescheduled debt worth a total of $308 million slated for repayment between July 1996 and May 1997.
The new accord should help Jordan reduce its debt repayment burden and cushion the impact of tough IMF-directed economic reforms. Currently Jordan pays around $500 million in debt servicing annually.
Jordan hopes that with support from the IMF and the World Bank it could get even better rescheduling terms from those it secured in 1994, officials said.

Marto said Jordan's total official debt stood at $6.4 billion of which $3.5 billion to $4 billion was owed to bilateral official creditors with the rest concessional loans from agencies such as the World Bank and Arab aid funds.
This excludes $1.3 billion of rescheduled London Club commercial debt which was collaterised in Brady bonds in 1994.
Jordan hopes its record so far in pursuing an IMF-directed economic restructuring programme will provide it with a symphathetic hearing from official creditors.

Jordan will argue to the Paris Club that it has gone a long way in meeting IMF growth targets and deserves favourable terms to ensure it can comfortably surmount major political and social hurdles anticipated as it undertakes advanced economic reforms.
Jordan will begin a new three year IMF-guided programme in 1998 expected to focus on accelerating the pace of economic structural reforms including rapid privatisation.

But officials privately say the country is not likely to get support for any outright debt forgiveness although they believe creditors are looking favourably at writing off debt in return for investment commitments.

Because Jordan has a per capita earnings in excess of $1,000 Jordan is classed as a middle income country which gives it less favourable treatment. Jordan's debt to GDP ratio has fallen to 90 percent in 1996 from a peak of 203.4 percent in 1991.
